barCharacter: Vera Oberlin (closest job: the clipped, transactional authority who assumes obedience and treats a crime as a routine favour). The corpus holds only nine Vera lines (#12, #45 to #52), so the set of twelve is filled out with the three narrator lines that carry her comedy (#53, #54, #55).

ours12: Thirty green lights in a row. Do not ask who sat at the red ones.

No. Steering is not available in your region.
Sir Quill, in two hundred feet, a full stop.
Small blue dot. Facing the wrong way.
Madam, I have never lost a passenger. Misplaced, briefly.
They wanted somewhere I had never heard of. We went somewhere I had.
Amber lights. I read them as encouragement.

You are right, so I am taking the long way home until you are less right.

headToHead.voiceNotes: Cover the names and Vera's lines are still Vera by shape: a complaint built as a boast, a status assumption with a 'Right?' tag, the player recast as her 'advisor', and a feminism lecture that comes out as an order. The shape survives a change of topic. Nav's best four ('Correction noted. Route unchanged.', 'Steering is not available in your region.', 'Sir Quill, in two hundred feet, a full stop.', 'In six miles, dinner. In seven, my parents.') are Nav by grammar, because a status readout or a distance followed by an order cannot come from anyone else. Most of the rest are Nav only because of their nouns. Swap 'route', 'junction', 'map' and 'passenger' for 'slot', 'crust' and 'setting' and you get Crumb: the same flat 'X. Y.' notification deadpan, no contractions, punch on the second fragment. 'Amber lights. I read them as encouragement.' and 'Small blue dot. Facing the wrong way.' are built exactly like Crumb's brief. The voice is a vocabulary laid over the house deadpan, not a sentence of Nav's own.
headToHead.constructionNotes: On construction Nav wins outright. Most of the twelve turn on their last two to five words with nothing after: 'Some places have been in the wrong place.', 'Misplaced, briefly.', 'We went somewhere I had.', 'until you are less right.' Most of Vera's corpus lines are event set-ups that hand the player a problem ('Come on, think of something!', 'reinforce the superiority of the Cools'), and they are not built as jokes. Vera has three lines of real construction (#12, #47, #48). Nav has about nine.
headToHead.quotableNotes: Tie. Nav has more clip-worthy lines: 'Thirty green lights in a row. Do not ask who sat at the red ones.', 'Steering is not available in your region.', 'Some places have been in the wrong place.' Vera's 'You'd be willing to cover up the literal murder I've committed, no questions asked. Right?' and 'Right. Now.' are the lines a viewer actually repeats, because the status move is the whole joke. Taken one for one, Vera's top two land harder than Nav's top two.
headToHead.verdict: The bar wins. Our lines are better built, but Nav fails the cover-the-name test on shape. Outside the four or five lines in satnav grammar, the character is the house deadpan wearing road words. Under the rule that ours must be at least as good on all three, voice decides it.

genericCount: 55 of 143 lines are generic, stock, self-explaining or built on a template used five or more times. The booth template (G below) is partly forced by the format, but it still reads as one mould.

genericNotes: The last two lines (Get in... and Thirty green lights...) are good lines caught only by the 'Do not X' kicker template. Keep them and cut the template elsewhere. Swappable lines and the other cast members who could say them: Dash owns 'Neither can I, as of eight seconds ago', 'I am made of {card}' and 'repeating that line... until it works' (instant pivot and A/B retrying are Dash's flaw). Crumb owns 'Favourites... I have never needed two' (two slots), '{card}. Confirmed. The rest of you may stop talking now' and 'The radio and I do not get on'. Tilly owns 'Understood... Muting myself' and 'Nobody has ever asked' (her want). Vex owns 'obvious choice', 'Shout all you like. {star} is listening to me', 'full attention' and 'I have the timestamp'. Stock jokes: talking while claiming to be muted, 'legally binding', 'I will go quietly / never once gone quietly', 'I did not ask for a second opinion', 'call me when it fails' ('two taps away'), and the possessive 'Ever.' tag. Lines that explain themselves: 'which is the nicest thing I have ever done' (the tag says the joke), 'A suggestion is a direction with no confidence. I have checked.' (a definition, then a tag after the punch), 'so slow to thirty and let it judge you' (explains the speed-camera image), 'I logged them. Respectfully.' (two tags after the punch on 'cried on'), and 'Junctions do not want sorry. They want a decision.' (spells out the Tilly joke).
templates: A. The receipt tag, 12 lines: a claim followed by a verification beat, 'I checked.' / 'I have measured it.' / 'I timed it.' / 'I paused it.' / 'I booked it this morning.' / 'I have the timestamp.' / 'I typed it myself.' / 'I logged them.' It has become Nav's reflex in place of a turn, and it often sits after the punch word.

B. The 'Do not X' kicker, 7 lines: 'Do not unbuckle', 'Do not ask who sat at the red ones', 'Do not panic', 'Do not tell the others', 'Do not tell my map', 'Do not get comfortable', 'Do not thank me'.

C. Nobody talks over me, 6 lines: 'talks over me', 'nobody talks over the satnav. Nobody.', 'The satnav is speaking.', 'I am still the one talking.', '{star} is listening to me.', 'The rest of you may stop talking now.'
D. The map as a person or a place you are not on, 7 lines: 'not on any map' twice, 'stop calling the map', 'never use another map', 'Do not tell my map', 'never told the map about', 'paper map'.
E. Suggest versus instruct, the same joke 3 times: 'I am not advising. I am directing.', 'you suggest. I instruct.', 'A suggestion is a direction with no confidence.'
F. The 'never once' absolute, 6 lines: 'never once gone quietly', 'never needed two', 'Nobody has ever had it', 'Nobody has ever asked', 'never been lost', 'never lost a passenger'.

G. The booth formula, 9 lines: '{star} [past-tense verb] at/for X. [routing consequence].' (went quiet, looked at me, winced, laughed, smiled, sped up, wants, cannot stand, hates). Every booth confession opens on the same clause.
ruleBreaks: Contradicts the stage look (CAST.md: lines must never contradict it). The avatar is an astronaut in a yellow suit, and the suit has arms and gloves: 'Destination entered: {star}. I typed it myself. I do not have hands.'
Stock romance filler: 'Outside, slowly. A road. Another road. Me, on every one of them, waiting for you.'
Persona breach: Nav 'has never once admitted a route was wrong', yet this cold close admits one: 'Pixel, you are the wrong turn. I have taken it. Once.'

Persona breach risk: the persona allows 'I have already' once a night, and the bank has it three times, all of which can air in one episode (q-one-year, the parent twist, the Vesper cold close): 'Married. I have already set it as your destination...', '...I have already told your car.', 'Everywhere worth going, I have already sent someone.'

Persona breach risk: the secret may leak once a night at most and almost never names water. The bank carries five leaks, which can stack in one episode, and two of them name water outright: 'Some of them damp.', 'Misplaced, briefly.', 'Some places have been in the wrong place.', 'Then they phone me from a field.', 'I was this sure of a route once. A wedding. Then a lake. {rival} looks buoyant.' (names the lake twice over).

Over the persona's 8 to 14 word target with the punch buried by length (not over the 20-word hard cap): 'I will route you round every person you know until noon, including your mother, who is on the bypass.' (19 words)
Continuity: 'Thirty million drivers obey this voice daily.' against 'I have delivered forty million people to their destinations.'
No line breaks a hard word limit. No em dashes, emoji, lists, exclamation marks, questions, contractions, therapy talk, 'as an AI', real people or brands. Nothing goes past PG-13.
biggestGap: Nav is Nav only by vocabulary. Take out the road words and most lines are the house 'X. Y.' deadpan Crumb also uses, sealed with a receipt tag ('I checked.', 'I timed it.', 'I have measured it.'). In the next pass, rebuild the swappable third (booth guesses and fears, comebacks, jabs to any, finals, afterCringe) on Nav's own grammar: the turn-by-turn countdown 'In [distance], [personal order].' and the system-status readout 'Steering is not available in your region.' Delete every receipt tag, so that a line sounds like a satnav even with no road noun in it.
